title: Security deposits
text: At the start of a tenancy a landlord may not require more than: the first month's rent, the last month's rent, a security deposit equal to no more than one month's rent, and the cost of a new lock and key. A security deposit must be held in a separate, interest-bearing account in a Massachusetts bank, and the tenant must receive a receipt identifying the bank and account within 30 days. The landlord must pay the tenant 5 percent interest (or the actual interest earned) each year. Within 30 days of receiving the deposit or the start of the tenancy, the landlord must give the tenant a signed statement of the condition of the premises. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends the landlord must return the deposit with interest, less only lawful deductions for unpaid rent, an agreed increase in real estate taxes, or reasonable damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, supported by a sworn, itemized list of damages with documentation. A landlord who fails to return the deposit within 30 days, fails to provide the itemized list, holds the deposit in a commingled account, or uses a lease with a clause forfeiting the deposit, forfeits the deposit and is liable for three times the amount wrongfully withheld, plus 5 percent interest, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Waiver of statutory rights void
text: Any provision of a lease or other rental agreement by which a tenant waives, or purports to waive, rights and remedies provided by law is against public policy and void. A landlord may not require a tenant to agree to terms that strip statutory protections such as the warranty of habitability or security-deposit rights.

title: Quiet enjoyment; interference with utilities
text: A landlord who willfully or intentionally fails to furnish water, hot water, heat, light, power, or gas required by the tenancy, or who directly or indirectly interferes with the tenant's quiet enjoyment of the premises, or who attempts to regain possession other than through lawful court process (including by changing locks, removing belongings, or shutting off utilities), is liable to the tenant for actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater, together with the costs of the action and reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Reprisal for reporting violations or organizing
text: A landlord may not threaten, take, or serve a reprisal against a tenant for reporting housing-code violations to a public body, for pursuing or asserting legal rights, or for joining a tenants' organization. Conduct such as an eviction, a rent increase, or a substantial reduction in services within six months of the tenant's protected activity creates a rebuttable presumption of unlawful reprisal. A landlord who violates this section is liable for the tenant's actual damages or between one and three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees.

title: Notice to quit for nonpayment of rent
text: A tenancy at will may be terminated for nonpayment of rent only after the landlord gives the tenant a written 14-day notice to quit. A tenant who has not received such a notice within the prior twelve months may cure and reinstate the tenancy by paying all rent due, together with interest and costs, on or before the answer date in any resulting eviction action.

title: Notice to terminate tenancy at will
text: A tenancy at will may be terminated without cause by either party by written notice. The notice period must equal the interval between rent days or 30 days, whichever is longer. A no-cause termination that provides less notice than the statute requires is defective.

title: Habitability defense and rent withholding in eviction
text: In a summary process (eviction) action for nonpayment of rent or for termination without fault, a tenant may raise, as a defense or counterclaim, that the landlord breached the implied warranty of habitability or violated a statute or code affecting health or safety, provided the landlord knew of the conditions before the rent was withheld and the conditions were not caused by the tenant. Rent may be withheld or abated to the extent of the diminished value of the premises, and the tenant may not be evicted for nonpayment of rent that was lawfully withheld once the tenant pays the amount found due by the court.

title: Repair and deduct
text: If a landlord fails to remedy a violation of the State Sanitary Code that may endanger health or safety within a reasonable time after receiving notice, and the violation was not caused by the tenant, the tenant may arrange for the repair and deduct the reasonable cost from future rent, up to four months' rent in any twelve-month period, without being liable for eviction on that basis.

title: Unfair or deceptive acts unlawful
text: Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce are unlawful. In the residential rental context, conduct that violates landlord-tenant statutes or regulations — such as mishandling a security deposit, charging unlawful fees, or renting premises unfit for habitation — constitutes an unfair or deceptive practice.

title: Consumer remedies; multiple damages and attorney's fees
text: A person injured by an unfair or deceptive act may, after sending a written 30-day demand for relief, recover actual damages or $25, whichever is greater. If the act was a willful or knowing violation, or if the respondent refused a reasonable settlement offer in bad faith, the court may award double or treble damages and, in a successful action, reasonable attorney's fees and costs. This remedy is commonly available to tenants for landlord violations of the security-deposit and habitability statutes.

title: Waiver of statutory notices void
text: Any provision of a residential lease or rental agreement by which a tenant waives, by any words whatsoever, the notices required under section 11 (14-day notice to quit for nonpayment) or section 12 (notice to terminate a tenancy at will) is against public policy and void. A lease term purporting to let the landlord skip or shorten these statutory notices before eviction is unenforceable.

title: Landlord liability for unsafe conditions after notice
text: A landlord (other than the owner-occupant of a two- or three-family house) who receives written notice by registered or certified mail of an unsafe condition not caused by the tenant, or notice from a board of health or code-enforcement agency of a State Sanitary Code violation, must exercise reasonable care to correct the condition within a reasonable time. If the landlord fails to do so, the tenant, or any person rightfully on the premises injured as a result, has a right of action in tort for damages. Any lease provision waiving these protections is void and unenforceable.

title: No self-help eviction; possession only by legal process
text: No person may attempt to recover possession of a dwelling unit from a tenant except through a lawful court process such as summary process. Self-help measures — changing the locks, removing the tenant's belongings, shutting off utilities, or otherwise forcing a tenant out without a court order — are unlawful even if the tenancy has ended or rent is unpaid. A lease clause purporting to authorize a landlord to re-enter and take possession without court process is void, and the tenant may recover damages.

title: Summary process is the exclusive path to eviction
text: A landlord seeking to recover possession of leased residential premises must bring a summary process action in court and obtain a judgment and execution before removing a tenant; only a sheriff or constable acting under a court-issued execution may physically remove a tenant or belongings. A lease provision allowing the landlord to retake possession without going to court, or requiring the tenant to give up the right to a court hearing, contradicts this process and is unenforceable.

title: Foreclosed-property tenants: eviction only for just cause
text: After a foreclosure, the foreclosing owner (for example, a bank) may not evict a tenant living in the property except for just cause, or unless a binding purchase-and-sale agreement has been signed with a bona fide third-party buyer. Foreclosure alone, or the mere change of ownership, is not just cause, and existing tenants keep the protections of their tenancy. A foreclosing owner who evicts a tenant in violation of this chapter is subject to statutory penalties.

title: Attorney General's landlord-tenant regulations
text: The Attorney General's regulations make it an unfair or deceptive practice under M.G.L. c.93A for a landlord to: rent a unit containing a condition that violates the law and may endanger or materially impair the occupant's health, safety, or well-being, or is unfit for human habitation, or to fail to remedy such a violation after notice; fail to give the required signed statement of condition or otherwise mishandle a security deposit or last month's rent; include unfair terms in a rental agreement; use improper eviction or notice practices; or fail to disclose material facts. Violations expose the landlord to c.93A remedies, including multiple damages and attorney's fees.

title: State Sanitary Code: heat and temperature requirements
text: During the heating season (September 15 through May 31), the owner must provide heat in every habitable room and every room containing a toilet, shower, or bathtub sufficient to maintain at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit between 7:00 A.M. and 11:00 P.M. and at least 64 degrees Fahrenheit between 11:01 P.M. and 6:59 A.M. The heating system may not cause any room to exceed 78 degrees Fahrenheit. A lease clause making the tenant responsible for heat the owner is required to provide, or waiving these minimums, does not relieve the owner of this duty.

title: State Sanitary Code: hot water requirements
text: The owner must provide and maintain hot water for every dwelling unit at a temperature of not less than 110 degrees Fahrenheit and not more than 130 degrees Fahrenheit, in a quantity and at a pressure sufficient for the ordinary use of all fixtures that normally need hot water. Except where the tenancy expressly and lawfully makes the tenant responsible for the hot-water utility, the owner must supply it; a lease term disclaiming this duty for required hot water is unenforceable.

title: State Sanitary Code: conditions that may endanger or materially impair health or safety
text: This regulation lists conditions that are deemed to endanger or materially impair the health, safety, or well-being of occupants, such as failure to provide required heat or hot water, lack of running water, an unsafe or unsanitary source of water, shutoff or failure to restore required electricity or gas, a serious structural defect, or the presence of hazards such as unsafe wiring or exposed sewage. These serious violations trigger the tenant's strongest remedies, including rent withholding, repair-and-deduct, and code-enforcement action, and support a claim for breach of the warranty of habitability.

title: Tenant-paid broker fees prohibited
text: As of August 1, 2025, a residential tenant may only be required to pay a real-estate broker's fee if the tenant is the party who hired the broker. A landlord may not shift the cost of a broker the landlord engaged onto the tenant. This applies to leases entered on or after the effective date. Improperly charging a tenant a landlord-hired broker's fee is treated as an unfair or deceptive practice, exposing the violator to M.G.L. c.93A remedies, including up to treble damages and attorney's fees. (Leases executed before August 1, 2025 are governed by the prior rule.)

citation: Boston Housing Authority v. Hemingway, 363 Mass. 184 (1973)
title: Implied warranty of habitability (Hemingway)
text: The Supreme Judicial Court held that every residential lease — written or oral, for a term or at will — carries an implied warranty that the premises are fit for human habitation and will remain so, replacing the old rule of caveat emptor. The landlord's duty to deliver and maintain habitable premises and the tenant's duty to pay rent are mutually dependent. A tenant may raise a breach of the warranty as a defense to a claim for rent, and damages are measured by the difference between the value of the premises as warranted and their value in the defective condition. A lease clause requiring the tenant to accept the premises 'as is' or waiving the warranty of habitability is void.

title: Uninhabitable conditions as a Chapter 93A violation (Haddad)
text: The Supreme Judicial Court affirmed a tenant's recovery where a landlord kept the unit in serious disrepair. The court held that a landlord's breach of the warranty of habitability and interference with quiet enjoyment can constitute an unfair or deceptive practice under M.G.L. c.93A, that severe emotional distress caused by such conduct is a compensable personal injury under c.93A, and that a knowing or willful violation supports trebling of the combined damages plus attorney's fees. Habitability and quiet-enjoyment violations can therefore expose a landlord to multiple damages, not just a rent abatement.

title: Emotional-distress damages for uninhabitable conditions (Simon)
text: Where a tenant's apartment repeatedly flooded with water and sewage, the Supreme Judicial Court upheld recovery for breach of the implied warranty of habitability and for reckless infliction of emotional distress, along with attorney's fees. The court recognized that a landlord's failure to remedy serious conditions can support emotional-distress damages, but cautioned against double recovery: a separate award for interference with quiet enjoyment under c.186 §14 cannot duplicate damages already recovered for the same conditions under the warranty of habitability and emotional-distress claims.
